families.s: HSE hairdressing wet-work and dermatitis prevention guidance
families.t: water, shampoo, colouring, bleaching, non-latex gloves, hand drying, moisturising, glove changes and skin checks
f: Frequent contact with water and shampoo can irritate hairdressers' skin and cause dermatitis.
Hairdressing and cleaning products can cause irritant or allergic skin disease.
Disposable non-latex gloves should be worn for shampooing, colouring and bleaching.
Gloves should fit well and protect wrists from splashes.
Gloves should be changed between clients.
Hands should be dried thoroughly with a soft towel.
Moisturiser should be used regularly to protect the skin barrier.
Regular skin checks support early detection and reporting of dermatitis.
families.g: Hairdressing dermatitis risk depends on wet-work duration, shampoos and chemicals, glove material and fit, handwashing and drying, skin care, client frequency, susceptibility and early reporting.

families.s: HSE hairdressing asthma control for persulphates, henna and sprays
families.t: dusty products, persulphates, henna, aerosols, asthma, product selection, mixing, ventilation, exposure minimisation and symptom reporting
f: Dusty hairdressing products such as persulphates and henna can cause occupational asthma.
Hair sprays can aggravate asthma.
The workplace should be well ventilated.
Work methods should minimise creation and inhalation of dust and aerosols.
Products and mixing methods should be selected to reduce airborne release.
Containers should be handled and closed to limit spills and dust.
Workers should be informed about early breathing symptoms and the need to report them.
Risk assessment should consider workers with existing asthma or sensitisation.
families.g: Hairdressing respiratory risk depends on product and powderiness, mixing and spray method, ventilation, proximity and duration, cleaning, worker susceptibility, information and early intervention.

families.s: HSE glove selection and use for hairdressing chemicals and wet work
families.t: nitrile, vinyl, non-latex, cuff length, fit, changing, removal, sweat, skin reaction and client allergy
f: Hairdressers should use disposable smooth non-latex gloves for wet and chemical tasks.
Nitrile or vinyl gloves are suitable alternatives to latex for many hairdressing tasks.
Powdered latex gloves can contribute to asthma and skin reactions.
Gloves should fit snugly so they remain comfortable and do not snag hair.
Longer cuffs help protect wrists and can be folded to reduce liquid running inside.
Gloves should be changed between clients and when damaged or contaminated.
Gloves should be removed without transferring contamination to bare skin.
Glove use should be combined with hand drying, moisturising and skin checks.
families.g: Hairdressing glove performance depends on chemical and contact, glove material and breakthrough, fit and cuff, duration and sweat, changing and removal, skin condition and training.

families.s: HSE salon ventilation and product-control guidance
families.t: general ventilation, chemical vapours, sprays, dust, bleach and colour products, storage, spills, task separation and worker information
f: Hairdressing workplaces should be kept well ventilated.
Ventilation helps reduce exposure to sprays, vapours and dusty products.
Colouring and bleaching products can create skin and respiratory hazards.
Work techniques should minimise splashes, dust clouds and aerosol generation.
Products should be stored securely and kept in suitable labelled containers.
Spills should be cleaned using a method that does not increase skin or inhalation exposure.
Workers should receive product-specific information, instruction and training.
Control arrangements should be reviewed when products, salon layout or treatment methods change.
families.g: Salon product risk depends on chemistry and form, quantity and task, ventilation and room volume, storage and spills, skin contact, spray and dust, worker susceptibility and training.

families.s: HSE proportionate health-and-safety management in education
families.t: real risks, staff, pupils, visitors, contractors, sensible precautions, learning opportunities, review and leadership
f: Education employers should focus health and safety management on real and significant risks.
Health and safety law applies to school work activities and the risks they create for staff, pupils and visitors.
The law also applies to contractors carrying out work in the school.
Sensible precautions should enable learning rather than create unnecessary blanket prohibitions.
Risk management should balance employee safety and pupils' access to educational opportunities.
The approach should begin early and include ongoing review.
Typical school risks include transport, work at height, slips, violence, asbestos, maintenance and manual handling.
Leadership should ensure responsibilities, communication and controls are understood and maintained.
families.g: Education risk depends on activity and premises, staff and pupil needs, visitors and contractors, transport and maintenance, competence, communication, proportionate controls and review.
